claims.claim: Plotz compares Le Guin's clear, spare prose to Willa Cather's.
Burt: the narration invites readers in and holds them back, reminding them they are hearing a story and making them co-creators, collaborators, listeners as if to an oral tale.
claims.quote: co-creators, collaborators, listeners, as if to an oral tale

claims.claim: Burt names the clear, patient prose and its love for calm, open space, sky and sea, and likens the listening-and-waiting mode to Paradise Regained.
Tearle credits Le Guin with picking up the right word on the end of her pen; Plotz devotes a chapter to her use of language and naming and to the careful, deliberate nature of her prose.
claims.source: Oliver Tearle, review of Plotz (Interesting Literature)
claims.quote: the careful and deliberate nature of her prose

claims.claim: Le Guin reads the fundamental rhythm of LOTR as two beats — stress and release, inbreath and outbreath, a heartbeat — irreducibly simple yet capable of endless variation.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (summary of the 2001 essay)
claims.quote: Stress, release. Inbreath, outbreath. A heartbeat.

claims.claim: She lists pulsing pairs (darkness/daylight, confusion/clarity, trap/freedom) and insists they are not simple binary flips; each yang contains its yin.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (summary of the 2001 essay)

claims.claim: The narrative follows a physical gait — one, two, left, right, on foot from the Shire to the Mountain and back.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (summary of the 2001 essay)

claims.claim: She scans a chapter closely, hears its close 'like drumbeats', and recommends reading passages aloud.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (summary of the 2001 essay)

claims.claim: Le Guin (quoted) on Tolkien: even long sentences flow clearly and follow the breath, punctuation comes where you need to pause, cadences are graceful and inevitable.
claims.source: Vermont Softworks blog on 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: their flow is perfectly clear, and follows the breath

claims.feature: the writer must hear the prose
claims.claim: Le Guin infers from read-aloud ease that Tolkien must have heard what he wrote.
claims.quote: Tolkien must have heard what he wrote

claims.claim: The sound of the language is where it all begins; the test of a sentence is whether it sounds right.
claims.source: Literary Hub, 'A Writing Lesson from Ursula K. Le Guin' (excerpt from Steering the Craft)
claims.quote: The sound of the language is where it all begins.

claims.claim: The chief duty of a narrative sentence is to lead to the next; pace and movement depend on rhythm you can only control by hearing it.
claims.source: Literary Hub, 'A Writing Lesson from Ursula K. Le Guin' (excerpt from Steering the Craft)
claims.quote: duty of a narrative sentence is to lead to the next

claims.claim: Writers need a mind's ear; dull, choppy, droning, jerky, feeble are faults of sound, lively, flowing, strong, beautiful its virtues.
claims.source: Literary Hub, 'A Writing Lesson from Ursula K. Le Guin' (excerpt from Steering the Craft)

claims.claim: Prose's sound effects are subtle and always irregular (unlike verse); onomatopoeia, alliteration, repetition and dialect cadences are the tools, and changing sentence rhythms can express emotion.
claims.source: Literary Hub, 'A Writing Lesson from Ursula K. Le Guin' (excerpt from Steering the Craft)

claims.claim: The father tongue's essential gesture is not reasoning but distancing — one-way speech that expects no answer and 'only lectures'.
claims.source: Le Guin, Bryn Mawr Commencement Address (1986), text at Serendip

verdicts.trueWording: Her clear, spare prose reminds Plotz of Willa Cather's.
verdicts.note: Burt: 'Her clear, spare prose reminds Plotz (with reason, and I agree!) of Willa Cather's.' Claim's wording is on the page word for word; no quote field was supplied.

verdicts.trueWording: Le Guin invites us in, holds us back; co-creators, collaborators, listeners.
verdicts.note: Quote 'co-creators, collaborators, listeners, as if to an oral tale' is verbatim. Page: 'Le Guin instead invites us in and holds us back, reminds us that we are reading (or hearing) a story, making us co-creators...' — page says 'reading (or hearing)', the claim keeps only 'hearing'; subject is Le Guin rather than 'the narration'. Both are within paraphrase.

verdicts.trueWording: clear, patient prose; love for calm, open space, sky and sea.
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'in its clear, patient prose, its cautions against worldly power, its love for calm, open space, sky and sea, untilled land.' Paradise Regained limb also on the page: Le Guin's plots and ethics 'remind me as well of John Milton's Paradise Regained (1671) ... and Jesus says no, and stands, and listens, and waits.'

verdicts.trueWording: Plotz discusses her prose's care; the chapter covers language and naming.
verdicts.note: Both quoted phrases are verbatim: 'the right word on the end of her pen' (Tearle, borrowing Chesterton on Stevenson) and 'the careful and deliberate nature of her prose'. But the latter sits in a separate sentence about Plotz's discussion generally ('He is persuasive when discussing Le Guin's style, the careful and deliberate nature of her prose, and the way she creates an alien world through ingenious use of language'), not in the chapter list, which reads: 'a chapter on the \u2018simple joy\u2019 of reading Le Guin's work, especially her use of language and the power of naming'.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the chapter (as opposed to the book generally) is devoted to the careful, deliberate nature of her prose

verdicts.trueWording: two beats. Stress, release. Inbreath, outbreath. A heartbeat.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Every limb on the page: 'as simple as a rhythm can be: two beats'; 'so capable of endlessly complex and subtle variation'; and later 'the irreducible simplicity of the trochaic beat, stress/unstress'.

verdicts.trueWording: reversals are not simple binary flips; each yang contains its yin.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim ('[t]hese reversals are not simple binary flips'). Pairs on the page as 'darkness/daylight,' 'confusion of thought/clarity,' 'imprisonment or a trap/freedom'; and 'Each yang contains its yin, each yin contains its yang.'

verdicts.trueWording: One, two, left, right, on foot, all the way. And back.
verdicts.note: No quote field supplied; the claim's wording is verbatim on the page: 'A walking gait... we walk from the Shire to the Mountain of Doom with Frodo and Sam. One, two, left, right, on foot, all the way. And back.'

verdicts.trueWording: She reads the lines aloud herself; no recommendation appears on the page.
verdicts.note: 'like drumbeats' is verbatim ('They are like drumbeats.') and the close reading of chapter 8 of Fellowship, 'Fog on the Barrow Downs', is on the page. But the page's only read-aloud sentence is Le Guin's own practice: 'Reading the lines aloud I can't help thinking of a Beethoven finale'. The two occurrences of 'recommend' on the page are Nepveu's (a friend recommending the essay; asking for further recommendations), not Le Guin recommending reading aloud.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that she recommends reading passages aloud \u2014 the page shows her reading them aloud, not advising it

verdicts.trueWording: their flow is perfectly clear, and follows the breath.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim inside the block quotation of Le Guin: 'Even when the sentences are long, their flow is perfectly clear, and follows the breath; punctuation comes just where you need to pause; the cadences are graceful and inevitable.' All three limbs present.

verdicts.trueWording: Le Guin observes that 'Tolkien must have heard what he wrote.'
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. The read-aloud basis is the page's surrounding argument (Le Guin: 'it's a wonderful book to read aloud'; sentences that follow the breath; the blogger never stumbling reading LotR aloud). The page's verb is 'observes' rather than 'infers'.

verdicts.trueWording: The sound of the language is where it all begins.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, opening sentence of the Steering the Craft chapter; next sentence: 'The test of a sentence is, Does it sound right?'

verdicts.trueWording: the primary way you feel and control rhythm is by hearing it.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim: 'The chief duty of a narrative sentence is to lead to the next sentence\u2014to keep the story going.' Page then says 'Pace and movement depend above all on rhythm, and the primary way you feel and control the rhythm of your prose is by hearing it\u2014by listening to it.' The claim hardens 'the primary way' into an exclusive 'only'.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that rhythm can ONLY be controlled by hearing it \u2014 the page says hearing is the primary way, not the sole one

verdicts.trueWording: A good writer, like a good reader, has a mind's ear.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Faults list exact: 'Dull, choppy, droning, jerky, feeble: these common criticisms of narrative are all faults in the sound of it.' Virtues: 'Lively, well-paced, flowing, strong, beautiful' \u2014 the claim drops 'well-paced' but adds nothing. 'Narrative writers need to train their mind's ear'.

verdicts.trueWording: sound effects of prose are usually subtle and always irregular.
verdicts.note: No quote field supplied; every limb is on the page but assembled from four places: 'the sound effects of prose are usually subtle and always irregular' (the claim drops 'usually' before 'subtle'); the prose/poetry contrast in the same sentence; the tool list from the chapter's exercise ('onomatopoeia, alliteration, repetition, rhythmic effects, made-up words or names, dialect') plus Twain's 'irresistible dialectical cadences'; and 'the way the changing sentence rhythms embody and express the emotions of the characters'.

verdicts.trueWording: essential gesture of the father tongue is not reasoning but distancing.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim: 'The essential gesture of the father tongue is not reasoning but distancing-making a gap, a space, between the subject or self and the object or other.' One-way limb: 'The father tongue is spoken from above. It goes one way. No answer is expected, or heard.' 'It only lectures.' is verbatim (of the written, college-learned dialect). Page is the 1986 Bryn Mawr Commencement Address, reproduced by permission at Serendip.
